title: Origins of cells
summary: How the first cells might have arisen from non-living chemistry on early Earth, from the formation of carbon compounds to RNA, vesicles and the last universal common ancestor.

keyterms.definition: The formation of carbon compounds from inorganic substances on early Earth before life existed.
No free oxygen and so no ozone layer, high UV penetration, more CO2 and methane, high temperatures, lightning and volcanic activity.
Experiment passing electrical discharges through methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour, producing amino acids and showing carbon compounds can form abiotically.

keyterms.term: Cell as smallest unit of self-sustaining life
keyterms.definition: A cell is the smallest structure that can carry out all functions of life itself; viruses cannot, so are not considered living.
The ability of a molecule to make copies of itself; needed for the origin of inheritance.
Spontaneous organisation of molecules into larger structures, such as polymers or vesicles, without external direction.
Enclosure of molecules within a membrane, separating internal chemistry from the surroundings.
A spherical bilayer that forms spontaneously when fatty acids coalesce in water, enclosing an internal compartment.
Hypothesis that RNA was the first genetic material because it can store information, self-replicate and act as a catalyst.
An RNA molecule with catalytic activity, e.g. the peptidyl transferase activity of ribosomal RNA.
Last universal common ancestor: the most recent organism from which all living organisms on Earth are descended.
A deep-sea vent releasing hot, mineral-rich water; proposed site of LUCA's evolution, supplying energy and chemical gradients.
Estimating time since divergence from the number of differences in base or amino acid sequences, assuming mutations accumulate at a roughly constant rate.

questions.prompt: Which was a condition on early Earth that favoured the pre-biotic formation of carbon compounds?
options: High concentration of free oxygen in the atmosphere
A thick ozone layer blocking UV light
Low temperatures and no volcanic activity
No free oxygen, so no ozone layer and high UV penetration
questions.explanation: Without free oxygen there was no ozone layer, so UV light and lightning supplied energy, and the absence of oxygen meant newly formed carbon compounds were not oxidised.

questions.statement: The Miller–Urey experiment produced amino acids from inorganic gases using electrical discharges.
questions.explanation: Sparks passed through methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour produced amino acids, showing that carbon compounds could form without living organisms.

questions.text: In the Miller–Urey experiment, electrical discharges simulated ___.
questions.explanation: Electrodes produced sparks to simulate lightning as an energy source in the early atmosphere.

questions.prompt: Why are cells, but not viruses, regarded as the smallest units of self-sustaining life?
options: Cells contain nucleic acids and viruses do not
Cells can carry out all the functions of life themselves, while viruses depend on a host cell
Viruses are too small to be seen with a light microscope
Cells always contain a nucleus
questions.explanation: Viruses contain nucleic acid but lack their own metabolism and can only reproduce inside a host cell. Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus but are still self-sustaining.

questions.prompt: Match each challenge in explaining the origin of cells to what had to arise.

pairs.right: Molecules that make copies of themselves

questions.explanation: Explaining the spontaneous origin of cells requires accounting for catalysis, self-replication, self-assembly and compartmentalization.

questions.prompt: How could the first membrane-bound compartments have formed?
options: Fatty acids spontaneously coalesced into spherical bilayers (vesicles) in water
Proteins folded into hollow spheres
DNA wrapped around histones
Ribosomes joined together to form a wall
questions.explanation: Fatty acids are amphipathic, so in water they spontaneously form bilayers that close into vesicles, giving a compartment without needing enzymes.

questions.statement: DNA is the presumed first genetic material because it can catalyse its own replication.
questions.explanation: RNA is the presumed first genetic material. RNA can both store information and catalyse reactions (ribozymes), whereas DNA has no known catalytic role and needs enzymes to replicate.

questions.text: An RNA molecule that acts as a catalyst is called a ___.
questions.explanation: Ribozymes are catalytic RNAs. For example, ribosomal RNA catalyses peptide bond formation in the ribosome.

questions.prompt: Put these stages in the proposed sequence for the origin of cells.
items: Formation of simple carbon compounds such as amino acids
Assembly of polymers such as RNA
RNA enclosed within a fatty acid vesicle
questions.explanation: Monomers form first, then polymers; replicating RNA provides inheritance, and enclosure in a vesicle provides compartmentalization.

questions.prompt: Why is RNA considered a better candidate than protein for the first genetic material?
options: RNA is more stable than protein
RNA contains thymine, which pairs reliably
RNA can carry information in its base sequence and act as a catalyst
RNA is always double-stranded
questions.explanation: RNA combines both roles needed for the first replicator: a template for copying (base pairing) and catalytic activity. Proteins catalyse but cannot template their own copying.

questions.prompt: Which is evidence for a last universal common ancestor (LUCA)?
options: All organisms have the same number of chromosomes
All organisms share a universal genetic code and many of the same genes
All organisms carry out photosynthesis
All organisms have mitochondria
questions.explanation: The shared genetic code and genes found across all domains are best explained by inheritance from a single common ancestor.

questions.statement: LUCA was the only form of life that existed at its time.
questions.explanation: Other life forms probably existed alongside LUCA but became extinct; LUCA is simply the one whose descendants include all organisms alive today.

questions.text: Genomic analysis suggests LUCA lived near deep-sea ___ vents.
questions.explanation: Genes traced back to LUCA suggest an anaerobic organism using hydrogen and inorganic chemistry, consistent with alkaline hydrothermal vents.

questions.prompt: Which kind of evidence supports the evolution of LUCA near hydrothermal vents?
options: Fossilised remains of hydrothermal vents with structures resembling early cells, and LUCA's inferred genes for anaerobic metabolism
Fossils of the first photosynthetic plants on land
The presence of an ozone layer on early Earth
Fossil mitochondria in early rocks
questions.explanation: Ancient vent deposits (e.g. in Quebec, Canada) contain possible microfossils, and reconstructed LUCA genes suggest life in hot, anaerobic, mineral-rich conditions.

questions.prompt: Match each approach to what it is used to estimate.

pairs.right: Age of fossils of early cells
Time since lineages diverged from LUCA
Possible traces of early biological activity

questions.explanation: Fossils are dated using radioactive isotopes in surrounding rock; sequence differences give divergence times; organisms preferentially use carbon-12, leaving isotope signatures.

questions.prompt: What assumption does a molecular clock rely on?
options: Mutations never occur in essential genes
All species evolve from each other at the same time
Fossils always form in the same rock type
Sequence differences accumulate at a roughly constant rate over time
questions.explanation: If mutations accumulate at a fairly steady rate, the number of differences between sequences indicates the time since two lineages diverged.

questions.statement: Estimates for the dates of the first cells and of LUCA are uncertain because early fossils are rare and rocks have been altered.
questions.explanation: Very old rocks have mostly been recycled or changed by heat and pressure, so evidence is scarce and dates are estimates with wide ranges.

questions.text: Estimating divergence times from base sequence differences uses a molecular ___.
questions.explanation: The molecular clock converts sequence differences into time, calibrated using fossils of known age.

questions.prompt: Why does the lack of free oxygen on early Earth matter for the origin of life?
options: It allowed carbon compounds to accumulate without being oxidised
It meant there was no water
It made temperatures very low
It blocked UV light from reaching the surface
questions.explanation: Oxygen would react with and break down organic molecules. Its absence (and lack of ozone, letting UV through) let carbon compounds accumulate.

questions.prompt: Order these events from earliest to most recent.
items: Divergence of the three domains of life
questions.explanation: Earth formed first; carbon compounds formed abiotically; cellular life arose, and LUCA's descendants later diverged into Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.
